claims.evidence: NHS Falls - Prevention: home adjustments and exercises for strength and balance can lower the chance of falling.
NICE NG249 interventions: falls prevention exercise programmes (progressive, tailored, delivered by trained professionals). Exact word 'offer' not seen in the returned excerpt.
NHS prevention text names clearing clutter and trailing wires, non-slip mats, good lighting on rooms and stairs; footwear that fits well with good grip. Stair handrails not stated.
claims.newSentence: Clearing clutter and trailing wires, using non-slip mats, keeping rooms and stairs well lit and wearing well-fitting footwear with good grip are among the home-safety suggestions.

claims.evidence: NHS prevention page advises regular sight tests; NHS page on free eye tests lists age 60 or over as eligible (England). Added 'in England' because the page is NHS England.
claims.newSentence: Regular sight tests are recommended, and in England the NHS provides free sight tests for people aged 60 or over.

claims.evidence: Retrieved lists came from NI Direct and NHS Inform (arthritis, stroke, Parkinson's, poor vision or hearing, dementia, low blood pressure; muscle strength and balance decline with age); not confirmed as an NHS England list, and medicine side effects not seen in that list.
claims.newSentence: Causes of falls include muscle weakness and balance changes with age, conditions that affect mobility or balance (such as arthritis, stroke or Parkinson's), low blood pressure, problems with eyesight or hearing, and dementia.

claims.evidence: Plain general fact; NHS Inform also reports about 1 in 3 people over 65 fall at least once a year.
Retrieved NHS text only says a GP or pharmacist can check whether medicines affect balance; the list of drowsiness, light-headedness, faintness not seen.
claims.newSentence: Some medicines can affect balance and increase the chance of a fall.

claims.evidence: NHS Falls page: a GP or pharmacist can check whether medicines affect balance.
NICE lying and standing blood pressure check in NG249 not seen in NICE excerpts (only a local trust checklist). Definition itself is textbook; 'shortly after' is extra detail.
claims.newSentence: Postural hypotension is a drop in blood pressure on standing up from lying or sitting, which can cause dizziness and may lead to a fall.

claims.evidence: NHS prevention: exercises for strength and balance can lower the chance of falling.
Tai chi evidence for reducing falls is stated on the NHS prevention page; walking and dancing not seen.
claims.newSentence: The NHS notes there is evidence that regular tai chi can reduce the risk of falls.

claims.evidence: NHS prevention: programmes should be tailored to the person and supervised by a trained professional; NICE NG249 says similar.
Duplicates c03; stair handrails not stated in retrieved NHS text.
claims.newSentence: Suggestions include clearing clutter and trailing wires, using non-slip mats, keeping stairs well lit and wearing well-fitting footwear with good grip.

claims.evidence: NHS free eye tests page lists age 60 or over; NHS prevention advises regular sight tests. Page is England-specific.
claims.newSentence: Regular sight tests are recommended, and free NHS sight tests are available to people aged 60 or over in England.

claims.evidence: NG249 covers people aged 65 and over and people aged 50 to 64 at higher risk; includes falls prevention exercise programmes.
Retrieved NHS text: a GP can run simple balance tests and refer to local services. Checks for muscle weakness, osteoporosis, eyesight and medicine review as 'GP role' not seen.
claims.newSentence: A GP can check balance with simple tests, review medicines and refer to local falls services.

claims.evidence: A falls team gives older people who have fallen or are at high risk a full assessment, and the GP surgery can advise on local referral (NHS Cornwall page). 'Availability varies' is inference.
claims.newSentence: Some areas have a falls team that offers a full assessment to older people who have fallen or are at high risk, and a GP surgery can say what is available locally.

claims.evidence: NHS 111 Wales: keep warm with a towel, coat, rug or blanket, shout or bang on the wall if no phone; NHS personal alarms page describes alarms worn or at home that alert a monitoring service.
Getting up slowly (roll to side or hands and knees, use sturdy furniture) and changing position regularly while waiting are stated; 'moving the parts of the body that do not hurt' not seen.
claims.newSentence: Advice for someone who is not hurt includes getting up slowly, and changing position regularly while waiting for help if they cannot get up.

claims.evidence: Vague 'seek medical help' with no route. Retrieved NHS wording: call 999 if the person may have injured their head, back, neck or hip, cannot get up, is confused, drowsy or vomiting, or has severe bleeding; NHS 111 if they may be in pain, injured or unwell; see a GP after a fall or if worried about balance.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says to call 999 if someone has fallen and may have injured their head, back, neck or hip, cannot get up, is confused, drowsy or vomiting, or has severe bleeding; NHS 111 can help if they may be in pain, injured or unwell, and a GP can be seen after any fall.

notes: The 999 / 111 / GP wording came from blended search summaries of nhs.uk/conditions/falls plus NHS Inform and NHS 111 Wales; the nhs.uk page text itself was not returned verbatim, so a human should confirm the exact 999/111 wording against the live page before publishing. The search did not return the main nhs.uk Falls page content verbatim, so its causes list and exact 'what to do' text are unconfirmed (c05 attribution to 'the NHS' removed for that reason). Free eye tests for 60+ is on an NHS page (England); Scotland and Wales have different rules. c02/c15 'offering' wording from NICE not seen verbatim.
